item.title: The College of Magic turns ordinary kids into confident, top-hat wearing magicians
item.description:
The College of Magic turns ordinary kids into confident, top-hat wearing magicians
October 25, 20267:24 AM ET
By
Julie Bourdin
,
Photos by Tommy Trenchard
Lubelo Mthenjana, who's 11, performs a magic trick involving fire during the annual junior magic contest at the College of Magic in Cape Town, South Africa.
Tommy Trenchard for NPR
hide caption
toggle caption i
Tommy Trenchard for NPR
Dressed in a sharp black three-piece suit and a dapper yellow bow tie, Lubelo Mthenjana stands alone on a dark stage, taking in the last few seconds of quiet before the curtain opens. He takes a deep breath as his name is announced. Then he opens his arms wide and flashes a bright smile.
"Hello everyone! My name is Lubelo Mthenjana, and I will be performing for you … some magic!"
The audience of about 30 children and parents is spellbound. They laugh out loud as he makes a string of paper clips vanish into a plastic cup and gasp with surprise as the clips reappear inside a matchbox. Then comes his best trick: He conjures sweets out of thin air and tosses them into the crowd. The room erupts. As Lubelo takes his final bow to thunderous applause, his mom beams a proud smile at the 11-year-old apprentice magician.

item.title: Archdiocese of New York agrees to $800 million settlement over sexual abuse claims
item.description:
National
Archdiocese of New York agrees to $800 million settlement over sexual abuse claims
October 24, 20266:47 PM ET
By
Chandelis Duster
St. Patrick's Cathedral in Manhattan, the seat of the Archdiocese of New York, holds mass on April 21, 2025, in New York.
Yuki Iwamura/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Yuki Iwamura/AP
The Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay $800 million to settle the claims brought against the church by some 1,300 people who say they faced sexual abuse from clergy members and lay workers.
Jeff Anderson, a lawyer whose firm represents more than 250 of the plaintiffs, said the settlement was finalized, pending signed paperwork, and that all plaintiffs had agreed to the settlement.
In an email sent to priests of the archdiocese on Saturday afternoon and shared with NPR, Archbishop Ronald Hicks also said the deal had not yet been signed but that an agreement had been reached with plaintiffs and their attorneys.
"We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors," Hicks wrote in the email.
